Undulating weekly loads (strength, hypertrophy, endurance days)
The same load, sets, and reps at every session for many months
A full recovery month scheduled after every two training days

explanation: Daily undulating periodization varies load and reps inside a week (for example a heavier strength day, a 6–12RM hypertrophy day, and a higher-rep endurance day). That gives planned variety for a general client without copying a sport-season taper. Static loading or month-long layoffs are not undulation.

distractorExplanations.a: A meet taper is athlete periodization aimed at one peak; it is not the default for a non-competitive professional.
distractorExplanations.c: Unchanging sets and reps for months is no periodization; variety has to be planned, not accidental.
distractorExplanations.d: A month off after two sessions is detraining, not a microcycle variation of volume and intensity.

prompt: After one successful session, a novice wants to add 40 lb to an 80 lb goblet squat. How should the trainer progress the load?

Begin daily 1RM testing because the client already adapted
Use a small planned jump (about 2.5–10%) and confirm technique
Stop resistance training and use walking until the jump settles

explanation: Progressive overload is a planned, small increase the client can still perform with sound form—often about 2.5–10% on a lift, or a small increment on dumbbells. A 50% jump (40 lb on 80 lb) is a form and injury risk, not a standard progression step.

distractorExplanations.a: Doubling again compounds an already oversized jump; overload is graded, not exponential week to week.
distractorExplanations.b: One good session is not a reason to start daily max testing; that confuses progression with constant 1RM trials.
distractorExplanations.d: Abandoning the lift after a greedy jump ignores the actual fix: a smaller load increase with technique checks.

prompt: A novice’s knees cave inward at the bottom of a bodyweight squat. You cue “knees out.” What is that cue meant to produce?

options.text: Knees tracking over the feet instead of collapsing into valgus
Knees shoved well past the little toes into extra hip turnout
Knees locked behind the toes no matter how the torso leans
Weight shifted onto the balls of the feet so they can sit deeper

explanation: “Knees out” is a tracking cue: the knees should follow the line of the feet so the hip, knee, and foot stay stacked. It is not a rule against forward knee travel and not a cue to spin the knees outside the fifth toe. Valgus collapse is the fault; mid-foot balance stays the goal.

distractorExplanations.b: Forcing the knees outside the little toes over-rotates the hips and can stress the knee rather than restore tracking.
distractorExplanations.c: Forward knee travel can be normal; the cue is medial-lateral tracking, not keeping knees behind the toes.
distractorExplanations.d: Shifting onto the toes is a balance fault; the squat should stay over the mid-foot while the knees track.

prompt: You set a novice for a conventional deadlift from the floor. Which start position is the best default?

options.text: Hips as low as a squat, bar over the toes, and weight on the forefoot
Neutral spine, bar over mid-foot, shoulders slightly ahead of the bar
Rounded upper back, heels lifted, and the bar hovering in front of the toes
Shoulders behind the bar, chest high, and heels raised off the floor

explanation: A conventional deadlift starts with a braced, relatively neutral spine, the bar over the mid-foot, and the shoulders over or slightly in front of the bar so the lats can keep the bar close. It is a hinge-pull, not a squat with the bar out over the toes, and the feet stay flat.

distractorExplanations.c: A rounded start loads the spine in flexion, and raised heels dump weight onto the toes.
distractorExplanations.d: Shoulders behind the bar and raised heels both move the bar path forward of the mid-foot.

prompt: A client is holding a front plank. When should you end the set as a technique fail?

prompt: A client overhead-presses by flinging the ribs into a large lumbar arch to finish each rep. What should you cue?

prompt: For a heavy working-set squat, which breathing strategy is the usual coaching default?

explanation: Minors cannot give standalone informed consent for recording that may be stored or shared. Follow facility policy: parent/guardian permission plus the minor's assent, before filming. Adult liability waivers and after-the-fact minor signatures do not cover this.

distractorExplanations.b: A teenager's verbal okay is not a substitute for parent/guardian informed permission to record.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent must come before capture and posting; a minor cannot ratify a privacy breach after the fact.
distractorExplanations.d: A standard adult liability waiver addresses injury risk, not media consent for a minor.

prompt: Two days after a novel high-volume leg session, a client reports cola-colored urine, severe muscle pain, and weakness. What should the CPT do?

options.text: Add a light flush circuit, extra water, and have them train through the pain
Stop training and refer now for medical evaluation of possible rhabdomyolysis
Add more eccentric volume because deep soreness means the work is landing
Recommend extra NSAIDs and schedule a harder lower-body day later this week

explanation: Dark tea- or cola-colored urine with out-of-proportion muscle pain and weakness after unaccustomed volume is a rhabdomyolysis red-flag cluster. The CPT stops exercise and refers for urgent medical evaluation. Hydration circuits, more eccentrics, or NSAIDs delay care and can worsen kidney risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Training through pigmenturia treats a medical emergency as ordinary soreness and delays a workup.
distractorExplanations.c: More eccentric load is how many rhabdo cases start; it is the opposite of the needed response.
distractorExplanations.d: NSAIDs can stress kidneys when muscle breakdown is already releasing myoglobin; this needs a clinician, not another hard day.

prompt: A client asks you to coach the snatch. You have never been taught to teach Olympic lifts. What is the safe action?

options.text: Cue the snatch from a popular video and keep loads at 40% of their clean
Teach only PVC-pipe snatches until you feel more comfortable spotting
Decline to coach the snatch until qualified; refer out or get trained
Coach the full lift anyway if they already know it from a CrossFit class

explanation: Competence is a safety boundary. CPTs coach only skills they are qualified to teach and spot. Until you have education and practice in the snatch, decline, refer to a qualified coach, or get trained. Light loads, PVC, and the client's prior gym experience do not create your competence.

distractorExplanations.a: A video plus a light percentage is still coaching a high-skill lift you cannot reliably correct or catch.
distractorExplanations.b: PVC work still requires the coach to see and fix faults; discomfort is a signal to refer, not to improvise.
distractorExplanations.d: The client's CrossFit background does not replace the coach's ability to spot errors and failed reps.

prompt: A client slips on a wet platform, catches themselves, and says they are fine. How should the incident be documented?

options.text: Skip any written report because no visible injury showed up at the moment
File the write-up within 30 days once you fully recall the sequence of events
Record your opinion that the client was careless and therefore at fault
Complete a same-day factual report with time, conditions, and actions taken

explanation: Near-misses belong in the incident log. Write the same day: time, location, conditions (wet platform), what was seen, what was done (cleanup, client statement), and witnesses. Facts only—no blame narrative. Delayed or skipped reports lose detail when symptoms or claims appear later.

distractorExplanations.a: Pain and claims often show up after the session; near-misses without a bruise still get a report.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting weeks destroys credibility and memory; incident notes are completed while details are fresh.
distractorExplanations.c: Fault opinions do not belong in the record; stick to observable facts and statements.
